title: data-cap: capability-owned data contracts
description: Your application's data should have an owner. data-cap declares each piece of application data once, as a capability-owned contract, whatever database, transport, framework or state library sits underneath. It works next to TanStack Query, Redux or plain fetch, not instead of them.
maturity: data-cap is pre-1.0. Per [VERSIONING.md](https://github.com/maverickcer/data-cap/blob/main/VERSIONING.md), a minor release may still change a Stable API before 1.0, so pin accordingly and read the changelog on every minor upgrade.

hero.heading: Your application's data should have an owner.
hero.lede: Fetching libraries dedupe requests. State libraries give you a store. Neither says which part of your application owns a piece of data, or what its status means to every consumer.
hero.support: A capability declares a piece of data with the getters, mutators and subscriptions that touch it. Every consumer reads the same snapshot.
hero.outcome: Give every piece of application data one owner and one shared status vocabulary, without replacing your database, transport or state library.

install.label: Quick start
install.note: data-cap sits under or next to TanStack Query, Redux, Zustand or plain `fetch` and `useState`. No database, transport or state-library change is needed.

problem.heading: Fetching and state libraries answer different questions.
problem.lede: A fetching library dedupes requests, and a state library gives you a store. Neither says which part of the application owns a piece of data. Neither says whether an optimistic value will disagree with other components.
problem.conclusion: no single source of truth for what the data's status means
problem.closing: data-cap makes the agreement itself the artifact. A capability declares its fields and operations, and every consumer reads the same synchronous snapshot.

model.heading: Full manual control, or batteries included: same primitives.
model.lede: `buildData`, `createDataStore` and `coordinator` are the same Stable primitives `createData` composes. Start wherever matches how much control the capability needs.
flow: → Manual path (Stable): `buildData` · `createDataStore` · `coordinator`, with full control over execution, retry and caching
→ Batteries-included path (Stable): `createData`, with dedup, per-operation status and an optimistic mutation lifecycle
model.flowDescription: The same Stable primitives can be composed manually for full control, or used through createData for a batteries-included dedup, status, and optimistic-mutation lifecycle.
model.note: Neither path is the one way: pick per capability. Fields are readable from the moment `buildData()` or `createData()` returns. `info` is on every `DataState`, so consumers never check whether metadata exists.

guarantees.heading: What it holds to, and where that stops.
guarantees.lede: Each claim states its scope and links to the document that defines it, so you can check the boundary before you rely on it.

items.claim: Ownership is enforced by dropping the write and warning in development, not by throwing.
items.scope: An unowned write is dropped and reported in development, instead of crashing the application. The warning never includes the value (tested for a string value on the `createData` path). data-cap is not an authorization or encryption system.

items.claim: The build tool never executes your code.
items.scope: Discovered files are read through the TypeScript Compiler API and never imported or evaluated. This covers the build tooling only, not your application at runtime.

items.claim: The two-module-system hazard is checked and documented.
items.scope: It applies when a dependency tree loads the package as both ESM and CommonJS, which creates two coordinator instances. A test pins the result: each stays correct, and dedup stops crossing between them.

comparison.eyebrow: Why not TanStack Query, Redux, or manual fetch-and-state?
comparison.heading: You keep all of them.
comparison.lede: data-cap does not replace your transport or your store. It adds one capability-owned contract that every consumer reads. A static pass turns that contract into ownership and dependency evidence.
comparison.caption: Where common approaches stop and data-cap begins
rows: No shared status vocabulary, no dedup, no optimistic-update contract; every component re-derives its own version
Says nothing about mutation-driven data your app owns outside a query, or how two consumers agree on ownership
One shared place to put state
Doesn't distinguish declared ownership from incidental access; anything can write anywhere

adoption.heading: From manual control to batteries-included.
adoption.lede: Most applications start with whichever primitive matches how much control a capability needs: full manual control (`buildData`, `createDataStore`, `coordinator`) or the batteries-included `createData`. Neither is the one way.
steps: Pick the primitive that fits one capability.
Migrate the next capability when it needs more control or less boilerplate. Each is independent.

notFor.title: You probably don't need it when
notFor.text: Your application is small, one team owns the entire data layer, and there's little reason to separate business capabilities from their storage or fetching implementation. A conventional fetch-and-`useState` pattern, or your existing state-management library alone, may be simpler.

brief.heading: A one-page brief for your manager
brief.oneLine: data-cap gives every piece of application data one owner and one shared status. Every part of the application then agrees on what the data is doing.
brief.problem: Different parts of an application each work out their own idea of whether data is loading, stale or changed. They disagree, and nobody owns the answer.
brief.whatItDoes: Each piece of data is declared once, with the fields and operations that touch it. Every consumer then reads the same up-to-date snapshot, whichever fetching or state library sits underneath.
whyItMatters: Components stop disagreeing about what "loading" or "stale" means.
It works alongside the fetching and state libraries a team already uses.
A generated report shows who owns each piece of data and what depends on it.
brief.whatItCosts: Adopting it means adding the package and declaring one piece of data at a time. It is free, open source software under the MIT licence, and it replaces no existing library.
whatCouldGoWrong: Security fixes target the latest 0.x release only, and there is no long-term-support branch before 1.0.
Ownership is enforced by dropping the write and warning in development, not by throwing. A mistake is reported rather than prevented.
brief.whatWeAsk: Agree that one feature trials it for a few weeks, then judge from its ownership report whether to extend it.
